title: Growing skirret
subtitle: A forgotten perennial root vegetable producing sweet, carrot-like roots each autumn.
excerpt: Skirret is a perennial root vegetable that produces clusters of sweet, white roots each autumn. It was common in English kitchen gardens before the potato arrived and is now grown mainly by those interested in heritage and perennial vegetables.
sourceNotes: Cultivation notes from Plants For A Future database (pfaf.org). Historical references from John Evelyn, Acetaria: A Discourse of Sallets (1699). Modern growing guidance from Agroforestry Research Trust species data.

glossaryTerms.definition: A root vegetable where the plant persists from year to year and produces a new crop of roots each season. Skirret, Jerusalem artichoke, and oca are perennial root vegetables. Carrot and parsnip are biennial and must be resown each year.

content.text: with sweet, white, pencil-thin roots. Harvest the roots each autumn and divide the crown to replant. It grows to about 1 m in flower and produces white umbels in summer that bees and hoverflies visit.

Skirret grows well in any reasonable, moisture-retentive soil in full sun or partial shade. It tolerates shade better than most root crops. Avoid waterlogged ground. It does not need a deeply dug or particularly fertile bed.

Sow seed in pots in March to April. Germination is reliable in warm conditions. Plant out when large enough to handle, spacing plants 30 cm apart. Alternatively, divide an established crown in early spring into sections, each with a growing bud, and replant.

Dig the whole root cluster in October to February. Each cluster produces a fistful of thin roots. Remove the roots and replant the crown for next year's crop. Roots can be left in the ground and dug as needed, like parsnip. They remain firm in cold soil.
Some roots have a fibrous core. Boil or roast and eat around it, or cut out the core before cooking. The flavour is sweet, with a hint of parsley.

attrs.title: Yields in the first year
attrs.body: Skirret grown from seed in its first year produces a small root cluster (perhaps five or six thin roots from a single plant). From the second year onwards, after division and replanting, each plant gives a much larger harvest. Plan for a productive patch only from the second growing season.
